 Palantir CEO Alex Karp Warns Wealth Tax Is Trojan Horse For Mass Surveillance
 November 10, 2026 8:18 pm 
 3 
 By Reuven Rosenfeld 
 Share 
 Facebook WhatsApp Twitter Linkedin Email 
 NEW YORK (VINnews) — Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp has warned that a wealth tax would function as a “Trojan horse” for mass surveillance, arguing that enforcing it would require the government to know the value of essentially every private asset a person owns.

 In a recent interview with Walter Isaacson for the series The Builders, Karp said artificial intelligence now makes such comprehensive valuation practical. “To enforce a wealth tax, you’re going to need surveillance because I’m going to need to know what the bench in your house in New Orleans is worth,” he said. “AI could impute every single thing you own.”​
 https://vinnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/TheChiefNerd_720p_20261110_191612.mp4 
 Karp, whose company specializes in data integration and analysis for government and commercial clients, acknowledged that AI is likely to widen the wealth gap. He has said the technology will raise living standards for average workers but could make those already involved in tech and AI “10, 20 or 50 times wealthier.” He called the underlying inequality concern legitimate, yet argued a wealth tax is the wrong response.​
 Subscribe to VINnews on WhatsApp 
 According to accounts of the interview, Karp contends a wealth tax would not meaningfully help the poor, would harm the tech industry by taxing illiquid holdings of founders and early employees, and would necessitate continuous monitoring of private property to determine taxable value. He has suggested alternatives such as higher taxes on high earners tied to reductions in government waste, or a substantial estate tax that avoids ongoing asset surveillance.​
 Palantir, co-founded by Karp and Peter Thiel, has long provided software used by U.S. military, intelligence and law-enforcement agencies. The company has drawn scrutiny from some lawmakers and civil-liberties advocates over its government contracts, including work related to immigration enforcement and tax administration. Karp has previously distinguished between data analysis conducted under legal warrants and broader, warrantless monitoring, and has said commercial platforms collect far more routine data on Americans than the government.​
 The interview, recorded earlier this year, is among several recent appearances in which Karp has discussed AI’s economic effects, privacy and the proper role of technology companies. He has described himself as an “unhappy Democrat” who criticizes extremes on both the left and right.

 The first problem with a wealth tax is the social conflation we have between wealth, income, and money that we have available to us.
 If a farmer owns 1000 acres and raises cattle on them and his farm generates $1 million a year in gross revenue, he may be doing pretty OK for himself at $300,000 a year net, But if the farm nearby recently sold their land at $30,000 an acre to a developer, then you may impute that this farmer has a net worth of $30 million. If you hit him with a wealth tax of 5%, that will cost him more than all of his take home pay.
